projects.title: Panel Discussion  Health 2.0 Conference  Dubai Spring Edition 2023 - Health 2.0 Conference (youtube)

segments.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I'm Ankit Shah and I'm a management consultant. Over the years I have advised senior leaders at pharma and biotech companies on clinical and commercial operations, organizational growth strategy, and lately there's a big boom in terms of utilizing advanced analytics and data technology. For this panel discussion, I'm focusing on global health equity, which I see is a very important topic to discuss, especially when we are considering from the lens of the next global healthcare crisis.
Excellent. And Mohsen, you wanted to talk about pandemic and health hazards.
Okay, that's very interesting. I think we need to delve into that in a little bit more detail to understand it. Dominique, you want to talk about mental health issues?

Yeah, no, I think, you know, all relevant points. I wanted to kind of, you know, throw a light on something called reciprocity. I think when we were tackling the pandemic, we observed that countries that had advanced healthcare and the reciprocity that they shared with the low and medium income countries, I think that was very critical. And I think when we are looking from the global public health perspective, we need to understand that equitability starts with the responsibility of these advanced nations to do more in terms of providing their infrastructure, sharing their resources, their talent to the countries they might not have the best or they are emerging. And I think that is one of the key tenets that I feel that was the lesson learned considering the COVID pandemic. The second thing I wanted to talk about is that going back to the equity in an utopian world, you know, any population cannot, you know, there should not be any barriers of any systemic or socioeconomic or geographic in terms of accessing the healthcare. But unfortunately that is not the case. And I think that goes through the three main areas. One is, you know, the global burden of disease. You know, there are a lot of unmet needs which we need to Understand, for instance, a drug that might have been, you know, approved, let's say, by FDA in the US There are varying number of years it takes until it reaches, let's say, Asia or Africa. And I think that itself is, you know, it's a tremendous burden on the disease. And, you know, how we are tackling, you know, the treatment options. The second is, you know, in terms of the infrastructure. So the government, you know, the Ministry of Health of each respective nations, I think they really need to do their due diligence in terms of the fiscal planning. I understand that, you know, funds might be limited, but I think with proper planning, we can at least optimize the use of the funding towards the healthcare. And I think it's also partly the interplay between the policies and the regulations that are set in place. A lot of times the access of the medication itself poses an immense barrier that the population is not able to undergo the treatment which might increase their quality of life or decrease the morbidity and mortality rate in that particular country. And I think lastly is the interplay between the four Ps, providers, payers, pharma companies and patients. I think we have to look, you know, collectively, a fragmented approach of, you know, tackling healthcare will not help. So I think these are the current areas that I feel have emerged, especially when we are looking, you know, the lessons learned during the COVID pandemic.
Thank you very much, Dominique, do you have any comments on the management and running of the pandemic across the world?

Yeah, no, I think it is definitely, you know, one of the areas that we really need to think and do more. I think if I have to, you know, look from the organizational perspective, I think what happened is that the lines between the personal time and the professional time, because everybody was working from home, it blurred. And while initially, you know, it was, you know, great that, you know, we were saving on the travel time, we were more efficient, but then the burnout also started to happen quickly. And I think that happened is because there were extended meetings, a lot of zoom fatigue and the decrease in the time of the personal time from the family, which was dedicated because there was a clear segmentation of the personal and the professional time because everybody was going to the office. Unfortunately, I think that led to a lot of increase in the stress levels and not thinking in terms of, or not putting a lot of emphasis that this can have a lot of repercussions to follow. So I do agree. I think what we really need to do change is that regardless we are working from the office or we have working from home, I think we really need to establish boundaries for ourselves of what we are able to, you know, you know, provide in a 24 hour, you know, in one day. And we need to kind of like think and understand that, okay, this is the commitment that I can provide, you know, to the professional time and then also look into, you know, some of the relaxing and, you know, the stress burning areas, be it let's say, you know, you can work out, you can, you know, do whatever hobbies that you're interested. I think these are very small little things, but it does, you know, contribute into increasing your lifestyle and, you know, bringing down the stress. So this is what I felt from, from my personal experience.

Yeah, I think, I think when you're trying to kind of, you know, look obesity as, you know, one of the crisis, I think there are few things that come into my mind. I think the first is how are we trying to kind of, you know, tackle. And I'm going to, you know, mainly focus on some of the developing nations because they have double the burden of fighting obesity, even though the statistics have been increasingly, even in countries like us. But I think when we look into a lot of these developing nations, one of the things that is lacking is in terms of the local manufacturing of the treatment options or the medications. And I think that itself poses a tremendous access to barrier to the access of the medications itself. You can surely try to kind of focus. And again, I'm just going to play a devil's advocate here. Definitely lifestyle changes make tremendous efforts in trying to kind of prevent. But at the same time, when we are looking into the patient population who is actually suffering from obesity, they need to get on the treatment options. And what happens is that because there are very few companies and there is very few manufacturing or the localization of the treatments available, these countries have to rely on other countries in order to access the medication. And what happens is that because the government is not looking from the lens of health outcomes, from the lens of access, there are certain guidelines, policies and regulations which are not conducive for patients to even get the treatments which is available in a lot of other countries. And I think that is something that we really need to change. A paradigm shift needs to bring and especially, let's Say, we have to think maybe if countries themselves do not have the means of setting up the manufacturing, there are a lot of opportunities in terms of, let's say, Dubai being an emerging health hub. If you look into, let's say a spoken hub type of a framework, Dubai can have relatively easier access to the medications supplied to the African nations, to the Asian nations, and also to the Eastern European countries. So we have to kind of see from the geographic point of view how we can increase the innovation hubs, how we can set up the manufacturing of these medications so the supply becomes much more easier. And I think that is one area where a lot of work that needs to be done and the focus has to be in terms of the pharma companies partnering and providing patient support programs, advocacy groups, specifically focusing in these countries which is currently not present.

Thanks, Sankit. So Mohsin, I'm going to ask you to be arbiter between these two individuals, one propounding that we should be spending more on obesity drugs and the other suggesting that we should be addressing the need and the education, I think from the outset to stop people getting obese. I can see the benefits of what you're arguing Ankit, but, you know, is there a role, for instance, for social engineering education? How would you approach the issue of obesity?

Actually, I'm a pediatrician and this is one of the major problems we are facing in our practice. The opposite of children. And for me, the obesity is not just a disease, it's a style of life. It is a way of life. How these kids are used to eat, how these kids are raised up, you know, I mean, for the mothers, most of, most of the mothers, for the time being, they are working mothers. And that's why, I mean, for them, the fast food, the quick food, I mean, the sweets, they are the main supply of food for their kids. You know, and too many mothers actually in the culture here and in other parts of the world, they love this, their babies to be obese. They love it, they enjoy it. They have the concept that, I mean, the more obese the baby is, the better the mother. And the mother is looking after the baby, you know. So I think not only the kids who need the education. I mean, the mothers need more education and deeper education how to raise their kids more than the kids themselves. The kids are very poor. Whatever you give them, they will take, whatever. If you tell them this is hazardous, they will not take it and so on. But we are facing huge problems with obesity in our practice. You know, the simplest of them, a child who comes with asthma and I need to put him IV line if he's obese. Oh my God. I mean, it will be really a very complicated task and I have to call the anesthesia to help me to find a vein for that child who the whole body is full with fat and how to dig to find, to find an access for him and so on. With all the statistics all over the world has been proven that the obesity in childhood, I mean, is joined with diabetes mellitus, gastrointestinal problems, mental problems, I mean asthma and bronchial diseases. I mean all is a combination with horizontal other actually which should be really stopped. Not with medication, I mean medication, I mean, cannot be given. I mean the medication how to. How to, I mean, to depress the appetite cannot be given except after the age of 10 years and so on, or six years and so on. No, it is how to change the lifestyle, how to educate the mothers and how to the children how to do it in a proper way. I think this would be the best.

Yeah. So population education, and I'm sure you do practice the individual point of learning that is always important. So as a breast cancer doctor, I always ask if you're a smoker and that is a very important learning point to tell the patient and their relatives to stop smoking. And here's a learning point that you can tell the mother to try and address the weight issue of the child. So education is clearly fundamental. Fundamental. My daughter is currently finishing her university course. She's been doing politics and history and she's been interested in the history of medicine, interestingly. And she was writing an essay on the interaction between the evolving data on smoking causing lung cancer in the 50s and 60s and the UK government policy on that actually not being very supportive because of the tax revenue. So a controversial issue, taxing sugar products. It's been discussed several times in the UK at the moment. It's been left to suppliers and producers to put labels which are of variable benefit. What's your view on taxing sugar? Ankit, you can start as you're jumping in there.

Yeah, no, I think it is a very dicey, you know, topic. Some may say that the proponents may say that, okay, you know, the government should take a stand and do what is right for, you know, their citizens. But on the other hand, it's also, you know, the prerogative of the citizens to choose what seems right for them. So I think when we are looking in terms of, you know, the tax benefits, especially from the government policy perspective, we need to kind of, you know, measure? What's the, you know, the overall implication that, that going to cause to the citizen in terms of their, you know, the healthcare itself versus the revenue that has been generated, you know, with the selling of, you know, let's say cigarettes and other relevant products. So I feel like it is. There is no clear answer to kind of like, you know, 100% impose a ban versus okay, you know, zero percent. You have the. But it requires a dialogue and an open communication between the population and the government and to understand what is.
Are you aware of anywhere that that dialogue has actually happened, anywhere in the world, is the dialogue actually happening between the government and the industry that is purveying the toxin?

So it may not happen at a national level, but I feel like, you know, in a pocket. I think Massachusetts has a great way to communicate, you know, with the population and to understand that what are they, what is their perspective? Similarly, I think, you know, California is also very proactive in terms of, you know, understanding what are the, you know, patients needs. But then you have, you know, certain states like Texas who just has a more authoritarian way of, you know, taking about part policies. So I feel like as a nation whole we might not be able to kind of bring one specific. And that is why it is important that the regional and the states take a very proactive measure. And there needs to be a little bit of, you know, dissection in certain policies and that we are also seeing in terms of the European Union as well. While maybe, you know, certain countries might feel that, you know, know, the taxing and you know, certain percentage might be something that really need to impose just as a part of a broader scheme of policies. But then there are countries which, you know, try to kind of look in more of a minutiae or granularity of their citizens and act accordingly.
I can see you're itching to jump in there. Dominique, go on.
Fantastic.
Thank you very much.
Public health crisis Pan.

Yes, actually it is, I mean, the fear of every guy who's living, I mean, in this country actually, and I'm sure in other parts of the world as well, that are we expecting really a second pandemic or not? And if. Yes, how we are going to face it and are we ready to face it or not? And I have, I mean, I have couple of points, points of views, to share it, to share it with the audience and to share it with the panelists as well. How we can, how we can really do our best to stop it where. Where before coming or before reaching to us.

Actually, when I revise how we suffered during the first pandemics, which has. Which has been, I mean, running all over the world, actually it was here in the United Arab Emirates. We have suffered a lot, actually, until we could govern it and we could stop it where it is. You know, I think the first lesson which should be taken from the first one is to study, I mean, what were the weak points which we have faced during the first pandemics and where were our weakness there? Not only in our country here, but in all over the world, in the different countries, what they were facing, what were the problems they faced and how they have solved. I mean, if these. All these problems and these obstacles could be collected together, I mean, and a committee could discuss all of this together to be able to avoid them, God forbid, I mean, if there is any coming pandemics. Because as you know yourself, actually, in case of pandemics, it is not the responsibility only of the government, it is the responsibility of everybody living in the country, how to fight and how to be ready for that and to be able to have the whole community, governmental as well as public as well as, I mean, insurance companies as well as everybody. It needs a lot of work. It needs a lot of work, first of all, to make sure that you are ready, really, with your resources, to face these pandemics or not. Do you have stockpiles which can be enough. Like the problem which we faced in the first pandemics. Actually, we were out of it. I mean, I would never forget that we, as Dr. G. We used to donate and to collect money between each other to be able to buy the masks and to buy the sanitizers and to buy other things, to be able to protect ourselves and to make it as a stock for the hospital. So all these issues which we have passed through, it should be studied, actually. It should be studied and we should put really a clear strategy for that. One of the big problems we have faced as well was the insurance companies. We were speaking about insurance and how the insurance behaved and behaving. Actually, insurance was not ready to cover any pandemics. I mean, that was an extra cost on the private hospitals as well as on the government itself. So, I mean, if we start from now, the discussions and the. I mean, the convincing of the insurance companies to be part of any. Of any pandemics of any. I mean, common things which are coming to the country which are out of the contract or out of the. It would be a great help to the whole. To the whole community, you know.

Yes, I think, I mean, the mental health actually is one of the most crucial points which should be stressed on if really there is any like the problems you have passed through the pandemics. Because if we study from what we have passed through, I mean, the fear of the people by itself brought them, brought them into depression and brought them into committing suicide, brought them into the fear of the vaccination where there were, where there was no transparency about the vaccination, where there were too many rumors about the vaccination. I mean, that brought the whole population actually, in addition to the physicians themselves, into a miserable state of mental health. Actually we were all depressed. We were all afraid that when our turn will be coming, you know, my colleague has been affected. He's in the icu. He is suffering between death and life. The other one, the next week was admitted as well, when my turn will be coming and so on. So this mental health, in spite of all the problems we were facing, it should be stressed on and it should be dealt with strongly during, during the, during any crisis or in pandemics. And it is required from the World Health Organization, from all the, the, I mean, the people who are in charge, whether ministries of health or to let the public contribute in decision making, you know, to let the public share the transparency. Okay, the vaccinations are necessary. They have side effects. Why shouldn't I tell about the side effects of the vaccination? You know, they should know the side effects of the vaccination. And each one then is free whether to take it or not to take it, but to make the things obscure and then after a couple of months to say, oh, it is causing meningitis, causing encephalitis, it is causing disabilities and so on. So actually the mental health during the crisis is one of the most important points which should be taken care of.

Yes, I do. We already had a couple of fantastic sessions here actually in the last two days as it pertains to mental health. And when we got this topic about global health crisis, there were probably three, four things that I could say let's talk about. And interestingly, they're interrelated, actually. But I believe personally the mental health crisis is already here. So I think we're living it, but I think we haven't recognized it as a global health crisis.

Thank you, Dominique. Yes, I agree with your assessment of the mental health crisis being here already. So the estimate is that one in four people in the UK will suffer mental health issues during their lifetime. That's adults and 1 in 10 children will have a major mental health issue. Also, I'm an oncologist. We suffer daily grief of our patients. The rates of mental health illness in oncologists has been reported variously as being 30 to 60%. Also, I think relevant is the fact that suicide rates amongst physicians are higher than the Population average. So estimate of suicide rates among male physicians is 1.4 times higher than population average and female physicians is 2.27 higher than population average. So I certainly agree that we are in a mental health crisis already. The other things I think we might consider are the current obesity crisis that is sweeping the world. I read an article this morning saying that if we actually use a more sensitive assessment of obesity rather than BMI using DEXA imaging of body fat, the current obesity rate in America is 75%. I'm sure it's not far behind in the UK. We're the most obese country in Europe. Also, I think one thing we might consider talking about is the workforce crisis in the healthcare industry, which is, I think, on us already. The successes that we've had for delivering treatments has put excessive strain on us and also has led to increasing rates of mental illness within the workforce. So how are we going to divide up the time that now remains of 40 minutes? So, Mohsin, could you just explain a little bit more about what you think is the pandemic issue that's coming towards us rather than the ones that we're in at the moment?

Yes, I think that's very important. Of course, the pandemic would probably have been classified by insurers as an act of God, which they were not responsible for. Ankit, do you have any considerations on this topic?

You know, it's interesting actually, as I'm listening to both of you, because these are big issues, clearly, and from my perspective, through my lens, looking at the element and the power of lifestyle medicine, it is so interesting to see the pandemic has shed incredible light on this subject. The pandemic has actually magnified mental health. It has magnified what problems we actually have. We also know if we went through the statistics that people who are overweight or obese were more likely to be suffering from the virus, etc. So we know that actually there, from that perspective, a lot could be done. So I see that there is an interconnectedness or exactly what you talked about. So lifestyle medicine talks about healthy lifestyles, which in essence, if I can be quite maybe direct, is free for the most part. So I think we're not utilizing a lot of these elements to bridge the gaps, which is so unique for this conference, because we're coming together to see how can we bridge the gaps, where are the connections there? How can we together bring that forward. So I guess as a last point to this, I think that lifestyle medicine could be an incredible key to a number of these elements of how to prevent or how to prevent repair as these things are coming.

Thank you, Dominique. I think we'll go on to that a little bit more just shortly. Clearly I can't really comment on the management of the COVID crisis in the uk. We're just entering a public inquiry into the mishandling in the uk and we know of course that, you know, we had major problems in our hospitals with access to equipment essential to keep our healthcare workers safe during the pandemic. And we know that nearly all of those involved in the pandemic, managing patients and seeing daily deaths, suffered major mental health issues. So I think that might be a good point to go on a bit more onto your topic, Dominique, of mental health. And I think what you're trying to talk about is holistic approach to the human entity that we have perhaps thought about health care as a separate issue. It has been raised in a number of other sessions in this meeting that what we should be trying to concentrate on is healthiness rather than illness. There's a lovely talk yesterday about the fact that we spend nearly all of our money on the 20% which is the illness, and we're not concentrating on the healthiness that we should all be aspiring to.

Yes, I agree with everything that you're just saying if I use this as an example. So interesting knowledge is not the same as putting things into practice. And I think we all suffer from that disease. We suffer from knowing a lot and not transferring it. And if I look at, for example, this conference, it's a perfect example, I'll be a bit critical. But most of the day we spend sitting, right? So we sit and sit and so we, we actually employ unhealthy lifestyle practices in our day to day life. And we're not acting, you know, as examples to maybe the patients or the people that we're working with. And I actually this morning too, I was trying to pull some more last minute minute numbers as they're there. And that's why I have my little book to tell you the true numbers. But a 2023 Gallup poll actually states, or a global study that 44% in the world of workers feel stressed, they are stressed at work. So nearly half of the people that go to work are stressed. Stress, we know, leads to a number of issues and so we're seeing an increase in all of this. The numbers say that mental health across, across all ages Genders, cultures have been, mental health has been decreasing, so the health is getting worse. And so the numbers are telling us that we are not implementing what we know. And I think this is really where right now the rubber meets the road is that what are we going to do with this consistent understanding and knowledge of the power of the simplicity too, of what can be done. For that we need to change the way we think about how we do things.
And how would you recommend that we do that?

Well, so first and foremost, I really think, number one for the entire healthcare community, I don't care from which sector we're coming from. I think an essential additional piece of being educated about what is lifestyle medicine, what are the key elements of lifestyle medicine and how can we implement them into our structure, into our hospitals, practices, workplaces, whatever it looks like in a real day to day basis. And that we can utilize the lifestyle medicine certifications for the medical health professionals for starters.
Excellent. Ankit, do you have any views on mental health issues and how they impact on workforce environments, on populations and how would you go about addressing the issue?

Well, really, like you just said, these things, of course, again are interrelated. The obesity epidemic has been going on for a long time. I spent over 20 years in the United States States, and you already mentioned it. It's one of the biggest issues that we're facing because of all the things that are connected to it. We now know that a person who is overweight or obese more than likely is physically inactive or not as active as they should be. Once you also study obesity, you know, of course that physical and mental health have a correlation there. So there's everything is connected around that. And the obesity epidemic really has so many victims. Every single year, we're losing more people to obesity than many, many other things that we focus much more on. And we are not utilizing focused interventions on that. So it's a complicated issue because now we would have to go into also the media and we have to talk about what's being offered and how our entire system functions. But the key thing that I believe in, again is that if we started to implement basic things also in society that are the norm. So for example, I use the conference, right? So if any academic meetings or meetings at work, standardized would be happening, standing instead of sitting, at some point it would become normal, right? And so you just mentioned it with a quote. It was brilliant. In our topic, it says the next global health crisis and how we can prevent it. That sentence means we have to take action. Without action, nothing is going to happen in terms of prevention, right? So we have to change the way we do the little things so that it becomes normal. Because if you think about the children growing up and the children watch us at the workplace, at home, we're moving. It's part of a daily lifestyle. We are eating fruits and vegetables as snacks instead of the things that we eat as snacks, etc. And so on, we would start making changes, systemic changes. And so to me, if we are not going to start doing. I'm giving just two examples of many, many on the list. But if we're not going to do that. We're going to have a severe massive crisis that's going to impact workforce, it's going to impact productivity at work, a massive impact on the economy, et cetera. So it's all a chain reaction.

I totally agree with you. So, Ankit. So I'm part of the Inequalities and Health alliance, part of the Royal College of Physicians and we wrote a paper to the government in the uk. Clearly there's an inextricable link between housing, income deprivation indices and health. And actually the biggest problems that affect health outcome are what social class you are in. So for instance, in the uk, in poor quality housing, often there isn't even the ability to cook your own food. So these people who are the poorest and most needy in our population are often using takeaways and all that. The health issues that that implicates and they are often the most obese. Would you like to talk about obesity as a health inequality?

Your question is a really, really good question because really the there we're talking about this, you know, the top down approach to make changes. And I am very much at this point in favor of these conversations to be happening. But like you already indicated, where are they really happening at a serious level? That's a question. And just to give a mini case study to that. One of my last tasks in the United States was I was a chief wellness officer at a university who gave me a job description to make the university the healthiest university in the world. That was my job description quite, quite big. And so I started to tackle the various different elements of holistic well, being the first one was to assess the cafeteria, of course. Right. And so I was at the cafeteria. They did a great job. They offered healthy choices, but they also offered lots of unhealthy choices. So going back to what you were saying, the student clearly was there and they couldn't make a free decision. The free decision of most students was every single day, pizza, French fries and Coca Cola. Okay. So then we surveyed the students, etc. And we actually pushed. And this was a long conversation. And this was not with, you know, the United States president, just the president of the university and the committees. It took a long time, in fact over a year and a half to have the committee agree on removing the sugary soda pop from the cafeteria and only offering flavored water options. Right. And here's the interesting part. The entire committee says we can't do that because people will be upset and so on. We did it. We didn't get one complaint from the student, not one, that there was no more soda. So this is very interesting. The policymakers had the issues, not the consumers. So just as a little case study of my experience at a very micro level.

Yeah. I think, you know, given an opportunity and given the knowledge, many people would actually choose the healthier option. I think I'll draw to close our time on the stage. But thank you everyone for your thoughts and your great expertise. I'll open it to questions from the audience now. We've got 7 minutes and 52 minutes, seconds. So on your marks, get set, go. That microphone. Any questions from anyone? So who. Okay, young lady at the front.
Okay, so this is the panel, not Andrew, because I know what's going on in the uk, so for the other.
Countries, go a little bit closer to the microphone.

So for the other countries, what I really wanted to know is in the uk, we've started with our primary school kids doing things like meditation. And it's all obviously very new to the more different generations. Do you do anything similar in your countries?
So I think the question was about meditation in schools.
Yes.
And introducing very young children to meditation. And is that an experience that you have come across, meditation?
And to be honest, I didn't know what it was, but I know my niece and nephew.
I mean, there are of course data suggesting that meditation in many instances may be as good as medication for people with mental illnesses.

Yeah. I mean, if the question is, as I understood actually, whether it's allowed in this schools, so I mean, to give the kids the medications, I mean, for each one of the, each one of the students I mean, there is a list which is written from the parents what medications he's allowed to take and what medication he's not allowed to take. You know, I mean, what allergy the child is having at what, and what are the things which he doesn't, which he is not allergic to. And normally speaking, in this part of the world, in the uee, before they give any medication to any child, except the life saving medication, they would call the parents and take their permission. Before they give any medication, they take the permission of the parents. Except, as I told you, if it is a convulsion or if it is something life saving, where they have to react quickly before and then inform the parents about it.

Yeah, absolutely. It's a very good question and it's definitely, of course, very sensitive the subject, no doubt. I'm personally a very, very huge supporter of creating positive social environments and also creating positive movements. So I personally would never, when it comes to. For the example you for mentioned with smoking, like you said, I would do it too. I usually challenge a smoker in a non smoking environment, but with any other subject, to me that's not the central focus. The focus is rather to employ a positive environment with positive practices because we know that social behavior impacts other people's behavior, right? So if we get more people to do it, I mean again, another example, if at a workplace, every worker at 10:30 takes a break together to go on a walk, even the people that never do it will start doing it because it's a positive behavior. So that's a much better approach, in my, my, in my opinion than confronting individuals on these particular health topics.
Ankit Mazen, any comments on this?

I would just like to end, I mean what I started with, with one sentence which came to my mind. I mean to the time of our prophet Muhammad Ali Abdullah Salatu. Salam. What he told us, if you want to live healthy, avoid two things. The two whites, salt and sugar. And this is coming now after so long. I mean it's coming true that if we avoid these two and if we are logic with consuming these two, we will be able to live healthier, much healthier than before.
Very wise. Words. Thank you. And thank you very much to the panel and thank you to the audience for attending. I'm going to wrap it up on on time.

So welcome, lady and gentlemen. And welcome, ladies and gentlemen. So we are going to try and discuss in 44 minutes and 46 seconds the issues about the next potential global pandemic. So I think, Ankit, you wanted to talk about health equitable access.
Thank you. Mohsen, do you have any views on.
